claim: The style guide was released publicly on DMs Guild around October 2018 as one of four free PDFs (IP guide, adventure guide, style guide, Forgotten Realms guide) that had previously gone only to official-play writers.
source: EN World — DMsGuild: D&D Style-Guides give a unique insight into the game (thread, 2018-11-25)

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that these PDFs 'had previously gone only to official-play writers' — the EN World thread says nothing about who received them before the DMs Guild posting
verdict.trueWording: Free on DMsGuild, 'only been on the site a month or so', four PDFs
verdict.note: Raw thread page 1 fetched (HTTP 200). Remathilis, Nov 25 2018: 'a rather interesting little gem that is free to download: A D&D Style-guide for publishing' and 'Its only been on the site a month or so' — which puts the posting around October 2018 — and 'Its divided into four PDFs: An IP Guide… an Adventure Guide… a Style Guide… and a Forgotten Realms Style Guide'. Those limbs are solid. Greps of the whole page for 'official play', 'organized play', 'Adventurers League', 'previously' and 'only to' return nothing. The missing limb is corroborated verbatim on this chunk's index-53 source (thekindgm.com: 'They were first available only to official play writers but now they're available to the broader public of the DMs Guild') — so the fact is sound but this citation does not carry it.

claim: The Kind GM's post on the creator resource carries a May 2020 commenter report that the material was no longer available, which the author acknowledged — so the public window was roughly 2018–2020.
source: The Kind GM — DMs Guild Style Guide Resources (2018-10-24)

verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'so the public window was roughly 2018–2020' — the page never says availability ended; the author's reply is that he fixed the link
verdict.trueWording: 'Apparently, this material is no longer available.' / 'I have updated the link'
verdict.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200). Post dated 'October 24, 2018 May 25, 2020'. Comment by mattwest2342, May 25 2020 5:43 am: 'Apparently, this material is no longer available.' Reply by The Kind GM, May 25 2020 12:33 pm: 'Thank you for bringing it to my attention. I have updated the link'. So the commenter report and the author's acknowledgement are exact. The inference limb is the problem: the author's response points to a working link rather than to a lapse, so this page does not establish that the public window closed around 2020. The page does support the window's opening: 'They were first available only to official play writers but now they're available to the broader public of the DMs Guild.'

claim: Work-for-hire WotC freelancers receive the D&D House Style Guide, the 5e Word template, pitch examples and lore documents at contract start, and drafts are formatted with them.
source: POCGamer — What happened? Writing for Wizards, Part 1 (Graeme Barber, 2021-03-23)

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the template is a Word template — the packet list on the page names only 'The 5e Template', never Word
verdict.trueWording: Receive an instructional packet containing: The D&D Wizards House Style Guide
verdict.note: Raw page fetched (HTTP 200; 'Graeme Barber / 23/03/2021'). Every other limb is exact. Stage 1 is 'Accept the offer, signing an NDA and providing payment information'; stage 2 is 'Receive an instructional packet containing: The D&D Wizards House Style Guide. The 5e Template. An example of a Pitch. Project Instructions. Project Appropriate Lore. An example of a pitch, draft, and extras.' — so style guide, template, pitch examples and lore documents at contract start, all confirmed, in a process the page frames as 'writing for Wizards as a work-for-hire freelance writer'. The formatting limb is verbatim too: 'Drafting Process: You will write a draft, formatted using the Style Guide and Template, and submit it.' Grep for the word 'Word' on the page returns nothing. The Word detail is corroborated elsewhere — the v1.04a style guide (this chunk's index-49 source) says 'If you are using the 5E Template in Word' — but POCGamer does not say it.

claim: The guide encourages contractions formed with 'not' (don't, can't, wasn't) and warns against ambiguous ones like 'who's' — a deliberately conversational register for rules.
source: Wizards of the Coast — D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (©2013; PDF hosted by the Adventurers League blog)

verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'a deliberately conversational register for rules' — the guide gives no rationale for encouraging contractions; the phrase 'conversational' appears nowhere near this rule
verdict.trueWording: We encourage the use of contractions formed with "not," such as "don't," "can't," and "wasn't"
verdict.note: The first two limbs are verbatim on p.3 'Contractions', including the ambiguity warning: 'Use other contractions with care, especially any contraction that can be misread. For example, "who's" can be read as "who is" or "who has."' The register gloss is the compiler's inference, not the page's. Machine-checked: 'conversational register' is absent from all 9 pages; the guide's only two uses of 'tone'/'conversational' are the High Fantasy 'general tone' passage and a separate rule allowing 'Dungeon Master' as a verb 'in an informal context, such as in a blog or a web article that has a conversational tone' — a different rule, not this one.

claim: Idle Cartulary judges the 48-page rules section plus 18-page glossary 'absolutely stellar information design' and 'an incredibly confident book', though terms like Influence action lack definition where used.
source: Idle Cartulary (Playful Void) — I Read The Player's Handbook (2024) (2024-08-31)

verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'the 48-page rules section plus 18-page glossary' - the 18 pages are inside the 48, not additional (29 rules pages + 18-page glossary = 'These 48 pages')
verdict.trueWording: 29 pages of rules plus an 18-page glossary make 48
verdict.note: Raw page read via curl. Both quotations verbatim: 'The organisation and use of the rules glossary is absolutely stellar information design' and 'This is an incredibly confident book.' Influence limb verbatim: 'the Influence action isn't defined in the social interaction section for example'. But the page reads 'It summarises the lot of them in 29 pages... helped in great part by the 18 page rules glossary in Appendix C it depends on. These 48 pages aren't just rules', and later '(compared to 48)' as the 2024 core-rules total - so the claim double-counts the glossary. Second, smaller slippage: 'absolutely stellar information design' is applied specifically to the organisation and use of the rules glossary, not to the 48 pages as a whole.

claim: 5e core-book editor Scott Fitzgerald Gray: mechanics editing needs precision in how a book 'fits in with the game as a whole', narrative editing needs flow and pacing, and prose editing serves 'the emotional language of the game' so readers feel like a character in the world.
source: Shadomain — Tales From the Tavern: Interview with Scott Fitzgerald Gray (2024-03-20)
quote: the emotional language of the game

verdict.unsupportedLimb: '5e core-book editor' - the interview never says Gray edited the 5e core rulebooks; it names Secrets of Sarlona (3e Eberron) and Vault of the Dracolich, and 'freelance editing for Wizards'
verdict.trueWording: Prose editing requires attention to the emotional language of the game
verdict.note: Raw page read via curl. The substance of the three-layer answer is verbatim: 'Mechanics in RPGs need a specific amount of precision and clarity, not just within a single book but in terms of how that book fits in with the game as a whole. Narrative within a book needs attention to flow and pacing more than attention to words. Prose editing requires attention to the emotional language of the game and how a book can make the game feel real, so that a player reading an RPG doesn't just feel like a player reading rules - they feel on some level like a character in the world that the game creates.' He names the three layers 'narrative editing, rules editing, and prose editing'. What this page does NOT establish is the credential: no mention of the 5e Player's Handbook, DMG or Monster Manual anywhere in the interview. Cite the credential from a credits page, not from here.

claim: Perkins on the 2024 DMG: 'everything in there better be cracking on topic'; the sample adventures use 'tight and short' read-aloud scripts to jog the DM's memory, avoiding his earlier 32-page adventures.
source: Screen Rant — 'Everything In There Better Be Cracking On Topic': D&D Designers Talk The 2024 DMG (Perkins & Wyatt interview, 2024-10-25)

verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'read-aloud scripts' - the page says the sample adventures are 'scripts for the DM to just to jog their memory', i.e. DM-facing, not read-aloud/boxed text for players
verdict.trueWording: scripts for the DM to just to jog their memory
verdict.note: Raw page read via curl (Screen Rant interview, Ben Brosofsky, Oct 25 2024). Perkins verbatim: 'everything in there better be cracking on topic and directed at DMs who are either new or who are looking for ways as experienced DMs to make their games more interesting.' And: 'I remember I was taught that an adventure was like a 32-page publishable thing. And so all of my home adventures I wrote as like 32-page things, fully written out... And so if I had the 2024 DMG, which has sample adventures in it, which are tight and short and really sort of scripts for the DM to just to jog their memory and make sure that they're sort of remembering the pace and flow of the adventure, I could have saved myself a lot of prep time.' 'tight and short' and the jog-the-memory and 32-page limbs are all verbatim; only 'read-aloud' is imported by the claim, and it inverts the audience of the scripts.

claim: Justin Alexander: 'boxed text is often too long'; break 'freeze-frame' text into actionable chunks and stop at the reaction point so players respond before the world moves on.
source: The Alexandrian — GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls (Justin Alexander, 2022-08-01)
quote: boxed text is often too long

verdict.trueWording: I agree that it must be mentioned that boxed text is often too long
verdict.note: The quotation IS on the page but it is not Justin Alexander's. It appears in the comment section, in the third of three responses, by a commenter named 'Andrew' dated August 2nd, 2022 - 7:13 pm, whose next sentence is 'I also tend to agree with Justin's critiques here', confirming Andrew is not Alexander. The essay body (everything above 'Filed under: Roleplaying Games Comments (3)') contains the string 'too long' zero times. The claim's other limbs ARE Alexander's own: 'what you should do is break it up into actionable chunks', 'What we've identified here is the reaction point', and the rule against letting 'the game world continue to move forward past the reaction point without letting the players react'. Related: the chunk's feature label for this claim, 'attention after three sentences', also traces to a comment - mellonbread, 11:58 am - recalling a lost WotC devblog piece, not to Alexander.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the attribution to Justin Alexander: 'boxed text is often too long' is a reader comment by 'Andrew', not the essay

claim: Gus L.: a basic room key is five sentences maximum; longer only for puzzles and NPCs — 'no one wants to read a three page key'.
source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)
quote: no one wants to read a three page key

verdict.trueWording: Keys longer than five or six sentences can work, with a good editor
verdict.note: By Gus L., Monday December 19, 2022. The designated quote is verbatim (page: 'No one wants to read a three page key to a single room, written in the style of Undermountian or a 1993 Dungeon Magazine adventure'). But the page does not set five sentences as a maximum. It reads: 'Keys longer than five or six sentences can work, with a good editor, and an attention to ordering their contents, but that's a good basic limit. Longer keys are even needed at times for complex puzzles and npcs, but basic description shouldn't really get beyond a paragraph.' So the figure is five-or-six, framed as a soft 'good basic limit' that longer keys can exceed with editing - and puzzles/NPCs are given as cases where longer is 'even needed at times', not as the sole licensed exception.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'five sentences maximum' and 'longer only for puzzles and NPCs': page says five or six as a soft 'good basic limit' that longer keys can exceed with a good editor

claim: Ray Vallese's editor's guide devotes a section to 'using present tense instead of future tense' and to 'avoiding rampant capitalization' — two habits of RPG manuscripts an editor corrects.
source: Ray Vallese — Writing With Style: An Editor's Advice for RPG Writers (book page)
quote: using present tense instead of future tense

verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'devotes a section to' — the page lists both only as topics the guide covers, never as sections
verdict.trueWording: It covers such topics as avoiding rampant capitalization, present tense
verdict.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200). Both quoted phrases appear verbatim inside a single sentence: 'It covers such topics as using gender-neutral language, ... avoiding rampant capitalization, ... using present tense instead of future tense, changing passive voice to active voice...'. The page is the book's marketing page for 'Writing With Style: An Editor's Advice for RPG Writers' (45 pages, by Ray Vallese, 20+ years editing games), so the editor-corrects-RPG-manuscripts limb holds. Nothing on the page states either topic gets its own section; the only mention of sections is inside a reader review ('Each section gives solid advice'). No table of contents is published on this page.

claim: Lynch's most-cited rule as summarized: replace the abstract judgment ('a cruel bully') with the concrete action ('Manfred takes a leak on Tobias's bedroll'); aim for 'the telltale sensory detail, rather than the generic abstract trait'; specificity, not mere detail.
source: Into the Dark — Bryce Lynch's Adventure Design Tips Summarized and Explained, Mark 2 (Jon Miller, 2016-07-25)
quote: the telltale sensory detail, rather than the generic abstract trait

verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'Lynch's most-cited rule' — the page nowhere ranks this rule's prominence or citation frequency
verdict.trueWording: Go for the telltale sensory detail, rather than the generic abstract trait.
verdict.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200). Quote verbatim in item 21 of Jon Miller's summary, followed by the exact example the claim gives: 'Instead of stating "One of the guards in the camp is a cruel bully," say "The burly Manfred takes a leak on Tobias's bedroll, and then snatches Tobias's roasted chicken from his hand and quickly gobbles it down."' The 'specificity, not mere detail' limb IS on the page but NOT in the post the claim cites — it is a 2021 comment by 'Clever Munkey' ('Try for specificity not simply detail'), which Jon Miller endorses in reply ('Specific but not verbose'). The superlative 'most-cited' is the researcher's own framing, unverifiable from this page.

claim: tenfootpole grades language on a four-point scale topped by 'Succinct and evocative', lists 'Terse writing style' and 'Evocative atmosphere' as requirements, and states 'Boxed text is usually not a good thing'.
source: tenfootpole.org — Review Standards (Bryce Lynch)

verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'as requirements', and the four-point Language scale is not Bryce Lynch's — it belongs to a second reviewer, 'The Pretty Girl'
verdict.trueWording: What I'm looking for in an adventure module; Language 4 - Succinct and evocative
verdict.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200). Third limb verbatim: 'Boxed text is usually not a good thing.' Both phrases verbatim as standalone bullets: 'Evocative atmosphere.' and 'Terse writing style'. But Bryce's list is prefaced 'What I'm looking for in an adventure module may not be what you are looking for. I try to avoid giving a module a rating' — and the same list explicitly grades requirement status elsewhere ('Wandering monster tables are generally required'; an overland portion is 'nice, but not required'), so neither of these two is labelled a requirement. Separately, the Language rubric (4 - Succinct and evocative / 2 - Conversational but clear / 1 - You should have hired an English Major to edit this / 0 - Very wordy/incomprehensible) sits in a later section headed 'The Pretty Girl', a second reviewer who introduces herself as 'not the gourmand that Bryce is' and calls it 'My ratings system'. It is on tenfootpole's standards page, so 'tenfootpole grades' holds, but the claim's source attribution to Bryce Lynch does not. Note also the rubric spans 0-4 with four defined rungs (no 3), so 'four-point scale' is loose.

claim: Chris Doyle's essay (as reported): write read-aloud like a newspaper lead — immediate threat first ('GIANT SLAVERING OGRE'), secondary details after, lower-level details left for searching.
source: Gaming Ballistic — Ballistic's Report: How to Write Adventure Modules that Don't Suck (2017-07-19)
page: report on Doyle, 'How to Write Encounters that Don't Suck'

verdict.trueWording: GIANT SLAVERING OGRE is moving through broken furniture
verdict.note: The quotation is on the page verbatim, twice, and the ordering limbs all hold -- immediate threat first, 'the rest can be dealt with after the party has survived the immediate threat', 'use newspaper conventions - big details that are right in your face up front, and details later', and 'the more your party searches, the more paragraphs can be read.' What fails is the attribution. The reviewer introduces the whole newspaper-lead passage as HIS addition to Doyle: 'One thing that might be implied but could be made explicit' -- an explicit disclaimer that Doyle's essay does not say it -- and then credits the advice to someone else: 'In fact, Juan Ochoa gave me that advice about giving him art direction.' What the page does attribute to Doyle is the encounter checklist (read-aloud text, description and details, stats, how a critter fights, treasure, consequences and developments) and the balance line 'first, it goes without saying that encounters need to be balanced for the adventuring party.'
verdict.unsupportedLimb: that the newspaper-lead ordering is Chris Doyle's -- the page flags it as the reviewer's own addition ('might be implied but could be made explicit') and credits it to Juan Ochoa

claim: Tad Davis describes Campbell's economy method: bold for immediately visible items, arrows to hidden ones, indentation for stacking, omitting non-essential words, with sound/smell/breeze cues.
source: ars phantasia — On Useful Dungeon Key Entries (Tad Davis, 2013-12-05)

verdict.trueWording: Sensory line is a commenter's suggestion, not Campbell's method
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'with sound/smell/breeze cues' — not part of Davis's account of Campbell's method
verdict.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), Tad Davis, December 5, 2013. Four limbs verbatim in the body: 'the immediately visible items are listed in bold-face'; 'Arrows to Non-boldfaced entries indicate items that are only described if the players investigate'; 'indents are used to group the items and these items are listed in the actual order they are stacked'; 'Words that are not essential are simply not used.' But 'sounds, smells, breezes, etc.' appears ONLY in a reader comment by 'Emily' (Dec 5, 2013, 7:43 am), proposed as something the format 'would work very well for' — not a described feature of Campbell's method and not Davis's text. Claim carries no quote field, so no verbatim grade available.

claim: Designing Dungeons cites Courtney Campbell's target of encoding 'everything you need to run successfully in seven words'.
source: Designing Dungeons — Chapter 10: Formatting Room Descriptions (Josh McCrowell & Warren D)

verdict.trueWording: Page: 'everything I need to run the encounter successfully in seven words' — unattributed blockquote
verdict.unsupportedLimb: attribution to Courtney Campbell — the page does not credit the seven-words target to him
verdict.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200). In 'How can I write even shorter, punchier room descriptions?' the seven-words sentence sits in an UNATTRIBUTED <blockquote> (no cite in the HTML), and the next, separate paragraph says 'On Set Design by Courtney Campbell lays out an alternate pattern for keying rooms that is very terse' — i.e. Campbell is offered as an alternative to the quoted approach, not as its author. Also the claim's inner quotation ('everything you need to run successfully in seven words') is not word-for-word: the page reads 'everything I need to run the encounter successfully in seven words'. The 'tick room' of the blockquote is not this chapter's worked example (that is a sludge/funeral-shrine room), confirming the block is imported from elsewhere.

claim: Gus L.: 'Maps! Use them.' — never spend key lines on dimensions and exits.
source: All Dead Generations — Dungeon Design, Process and Keys (Gus L., 2022-12-19)

verdict.trueWording: Rule heading: 'Listing Dimensions and Exits is a Waste!' — with stated exceptions
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'never' — the post explicitly allows exceptions for exits and for Dungeon23 dimensions
verdict.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200). Quote verbatim: 'Maps! Use them.' is the whole line under rule 2. But the same rule says 'However, listing exits can be helpful if things are confusing, the entrance is itself important, or it holds some evocative detail like a taxidermy crow nailed to a door. I mentioned before that there's no absolutes in these rules.' and 'I also suspect there's some odd specifics with Dungeon23 that make including dimensions and exits more helpful'. The absolute 'never spend key lines on dimensions and exits' overstates a rule the author himself qualifies twice.

claim: Lynch faults Vallese's guide for saying nothing about white space, bullets or evocative writing — the DM must 'glance at the page and immediately find' what is needed.
source: tenfootpole.org — Writing with Style: An Editor's Advice for RPG Writers review (Bryce Lynch, 2018-08-13)
quote: glance at the page and immediately find

verdict.trueWording: 'He does touch briefly, in an off-hand way, on those'
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'faults ... for saying nothing about white space, bullets or evocative writing' — the review says he does touch on them, and frames this as scope, not a fault
verdict.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), Bryce Lynch, August 13, 2018. Quote verbatim: 'A core part of being perfectly organized is scannability ... the ability of a DM to glance at the page and immediately find what they need'. But the white-space sentence reads: 'This isn't a book on evocative writing, or even adventure organization topics like the use of white space or bullets. He does touch briefly, in an off-hand way, on those but not to any real extent.' — an explicit denial of 'nothing'. The faults Lynch actually names are 'editor minutia' and the alphabetical organization ('WRONG!'); his verdict is positive: 'It's easy to recommend this' and 'the only thing in the How to Write Adventures category that I'd recommend.'

claim: Perkins describes the 2024 DMG sample adventures' read-aloud as 'tight and short' scripts whose job is to jog the DM's memory, not to be recited.
source: Screen Rant — 'Everything In There Better Be Cracking On Topic': D&D Designers Talk The 2024 DMG (Perkins & Wyatt interview, 2024-10-25)

verdict.trueWording: 'sample adventures ... which are tight and short and really sort of scripts ... to jog their memory'
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'read-aloud' and 'not to be recited' — Perkins describes the sample adventures themselves; the words read-aloud/aloud/recite appear nowhere in the article
verdict.note: Raw page (curl, HTTP 200), Screen Rant, datePublished 2024-10-25, headline '"Everything In There Better Be Cracking On Topic": D&D Designers Talk The 2024 Dungeon Master's Guide'. Perkins verbatim: 'if I had the 2024 DMG, which has sample adventures in it, which are tight and short and really sort of scripts for the DM to just to jog their memory and make sure that they're sort of remembering the pace and flow of the adventure, I could have saved myself a lot of prep time.' The quoted phrase 'tight and short' modifies the sample adventures, not their read-aloud text; a case-insensitive grep for 'aloud', 'recit' and 'verbatim' over the whole article returns nothing. Boxed text is mentioned only by Wyatt, on a different point (adventures needlessly re-explaining what boxed text is).

claim: Encounters are keyed with labeled sections in a fixed order (Read-aloud Text, General Description, Creature(s), Tactics, Trap(s), Treasure, Development) and unneeded sections are omitted rather than filled.
source: Dungeon Submission Guidelines (Dungeon staff, Paizo, 3.5 era)
quote: The editors greatly dislike printing the words "This room is empty"

verdict.trueWording: Each encounter can include any or all of the following sections ... Do not include sections that are unnecessary
verdict.note: Quote verbatim: 'The editors greatly dislike printing the words "This room is empty" in DUNGEON.' The section names and the omit-don't-fill rule are fully supported ('Do not include sections that are unnecessary for a given encounter... the area is not an encounter and should not be assigned an encounter number'). But the page never prescribes an ORDER: it says each encounter 'can include any or all of the following sections', and read-aloud only 'generally precedes the other entries of an encounter'. The enumeration is also eight items, not seven - the claim drops 'Ad-Hoc XP Adjustment'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: fixed order - the guidelines say encounters 'can include any or all of the following sections' and never mandate an order (read-aloud merely 'generally precedes'); the list is also eight sections, the claim names seven

claim: Perkins says he almost always overwrites; his first Dungeon adventure was cut from 28,000 to 16,000 words.
source: An Interview with Chris Perkins, designer of Warriors of Heaven (Mimir.net, 1999)

verdict.trueWording: asked to trim the 28,000-word adventure to a more manageable 16,000 words
verdict.note: Quote 'I almost always overwrite' is verbatim ('Anyone who has edited my work knows that I almost always overwrite'), so the first limb holds. The second limb fails on the same page twice. (a) Outcome: 'I was asked to trim the 28,000-word adventure to a more manageable 16,000 words. I was not entirely successful; I think the final adventure came in at 21,000 words, still making it the longest module ever published in DUNGEON Adventures.' It was not cut to 16,000. (b) 'Umbra' (Issue #55) is called 'My first PLANESCAPE adventure', while the page names his first published Dungeon work as 'Wards of Witching Ways,' Issue #11. Cross-check: the Fraternity of Shadows interview in this same chunk has him in Dungeon #38 in 1992, well before #55.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: his first Dungeon adventure was cut from 28,000 to 16,000 words - the page says he was ASKED to cut to 16,000 but landed at 21,000, and names Issue #11 'Wards of Witching Ways' as his first Dungeon adventure, not #55 'Umbra'

claim: WotC scheduled adventure writing in 'MU' units of 32 pages or 20,000-22,000 words, about one designer-month each.
source: Baker's Field: Twenty-Eight Adventures (Part 1) (Richard Baker, 2015-03-09)

verdict.trueWording: MU was the scheduling unit used at TSR, not WotC.
verdict.note: Live blogspot page. Page: 'A "MU" was the scheduling unit used at TSR for RPG work. It stood for "module unit" and represented 32 pages of writing/design, or 20,000 to 22,000 words. When I first started at TSR, the standard was that a designer like me would be scheduled for 1 month per MU.' Quote verbatim and the 32 pages / 20,000-22,000 words / one designer-month limbs are all exact - but the page attributes the unit to TSR (Baker joined TSR in Oct 1991; this is the 1992 Dark Sun project), five years before WotC acquired TSR. The claim's 'WotC' is the page's 'TSR'.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'WotC scheduled' - the page says the MU was TSR's scheduling unit

source: On Writing Adventures (Mike Shea, Sly Flourish, 2019-06-17)

Omit verbose backstories.' appears verbatim, but under the heading 'D&D House Style Guide', described as 'This free set of documents from Wizards of the Coast includes the house styles the D&D team gives to freelancers. It includes a short paper on adventure writing.' claim: Mearls (2025) credits a collaborator with making sure a third-party manuscript matched the D&D house style, confirming an internal style exists even where none is published.
source: Grognardia: Interview: Mike Mearls (2025-08-27)
quote: everything matched the D&D house style

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that no D&D house style guide is published — the page says nothing about whether the style is published or unpublished
verdict.trueWording: making sure that everything matched the D&D house style
verdict.note: Grognardia fetched raw, HTTP 200; 'Wednesday, August 27, 2025', 'Interview: Mike Mearls'. Answer 8: "Ian Pace developed the rules and nailed down the technical end of the manuscript, making sure that everything matched the D&D house style and that our rules synched with the D&D rulebooks." Quote verbatim; the collaborator, the manuscript (Cthulhu by Torchlight, a Chaosium/non-WotC 5e product per the introduction) and the existence of a D&D house style are all supported. The trailing inference 'even where none is published' is the researcher's gloss — the page makes no statement about publication of the style, and items 241-243 of this same chunk cite a circulating WotC style guide.

claim: Bold is the only emphasis device, and a term already in the section heading gets no emphasis in running text.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that bold is the ONLY emphasis device - the page prescribes bold for emphasis in place of an inline subhead, and nowhere states or implies that it is the sole permitted emphasis device
verdict.trueWording: Use bold for such emphasis, unless it's in the heading
verdict.note: p.3: 'Finally, don't use an inline subhead when you simply want to emphasize a word or phrase. Use bold for such emphasis, unless the emphasized term or phrase appears in the section's heading. Then, no emphasis is required. For example, if a Heading 3 says "Ki Points," don't bold "ki points" in the associated running text.' Quote verbatim and the heading-term limb fully supported; the exclusivity quantifier 'only' is the claim's, not the guide's - the guide's italics rules elsewhere (pp.4, 6-7) govern titles, spells, words-as-words and unspoken discourse, and it never rules italics out for emphasis in so many words.

claim: In D&D fiction, thoughts and psionic speech may be set in italics, quotes, or plain type at the author's discretion, a reversal of the older policy.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: Aesthetics and clarity should dictate appropriate usage

verdict.trueWording: a change from our previous policy
verdict.note: Quote 'Aesthetics and clarity should dictate appropriate usage' is verbatim on p.6, and the discretion limbs are fully supported: 'In D&D fiction, authors are free to use italics, quotation marks, or no distinguishing typography to present a character's thoughts or psionic communication (see Chicago 13.43).' But the page says only '(This is a change from our previous policy.)' — the word 'reversal' is absent, and the guide never states what the previous policy was, so the claim's characterization of the direction of the change is not established by the page.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'a reversal of the older policy' — page says only 'a change from our previous policy' and never states the prior rule
